before.value: Administrators should be able to create, deactivate, and update user accounts; assign people to roles such as student, instructor, TA, or guest; create or manage course shells; control who can access a course or group; adjust permissions when instructors need extra help or when access must be restricted; and monitor activity to intervene if there is a policy or security issue. For shared cross-listed course spaces, the system should use a single common set of rules to avoid conflicting access, with any department-specific differences handled only through controlled role-based exceptions or separate subgroups so the overall course remains consistent. Role-based exceptions are especially important, allowing instructors and TAs to see more tools or manage submissions while students have limited access. Subgroup exceptions should also be allowed for lab sections, project teams, or accommodated students who need different materials or due dates. Ad hoc exceptions that let a single user bypass the course’s main visibility rules should not be permitted unless there is a formal admin-approved reason. Subgroups should be chosen by the instructor or admin based on teaching purpose, with the system requiring a clear reason; if tied to instruction delivery such as a lab or discussion, the subgroup should follow the course structure; if for collaboration, project teams are appropriate; if for accessibility or special support, accommodation-based groups should be allowed. Subgroups should inherit permissions from the parent course unless there is a specific approved exception. Administrators should only view the user data they need for their job, and anything sensitive should be restricted by role and logged for audit purposes. If they need to intervene in an account or override access, that should be allowed for support, security, or policy enforcement, but not casually, and only designated admins should do it. Some actions, like changing roles or deactivating an account, should require approval or at least a second review in special cases, especially if they affect faculty accounts or an active student record. One-off access exceptions are allowed only in exceptional cases, such as troubleshooting a support issue, resolving a grading dispute, or handling an urgent administrative matter, and they require documented approval from an appropriate supervisor or system owner, a clear reason, a time limit, confirmation of exactly which data or function the person can access, and full logging of who approved it, who received it, what they accessed, and when it expired. If unauthorized access or data loss is suspected, the system should immediately contain the issue by disabling the affected account or access path, preserving logs, and preventing any further changes if possible. Support should escalate right away to security and the appropriate NJIT administrators, and any notification to users or leadership should follow the university’s incident response and privacy rules. If there’s data loss, recovery from backup should happen where appropriate, but only after the incident is controlled and the impact is understood. Notification should go to the people who need to respond first, like security, IT support, and the relevant NJIT administrator, and then to affected faculty or students only if the incident actually impacts them. The message should be kept minimal at first, sharing only what’s necessary to explain the issue and any required action, without exposing more student data than needed. If there’s any chance the incident involves privacy or legal implications, communication should be reviewed before it goes out to the broader audience.

before.value: Administrators should be able to create, deactivate, and update user accounts; assign people to roles such as student, instructor, TA, or guest; create or manage course shells; control who can access a course or group; adjust permissions when instructors need extra help or when access must be restricted; and monitor activity to intervene if there is a policy or security issue. For shared cross-listed course spaces, the system should use a single common set of rules to avoid conflicting access, with any department-specific differences handled only through controlled role-based exceptions or separate subgroups so the overall course remains consistent. Role-based exceptions are especially important, allowing instructors and TAs to see more tools or manage submissions while students have limited access. Subgroup exceptions should also be allowed for lab sections, project teams, or accommodated students who need different materials or due dates. Ad hoc exceptions that let a single user bypass the course’s main visibility rules should not be permitted unless there is a formal admin-approved reason. Subgroups should be chosen by the instructor or admin based on teaching purpose, with the system requiring a clear reason; if tied to instruction delivery such as a lab or discussion, the subgroup should follow the course structure; if for collaboration, project teams are appropriate; if for accessibility or special support, accommodation-based groups should be allowed. Subgroups should inherit permissions from the parent course unless there is a specific approved exception. Administrators should only view the user data they need for their job, and anything sensitive should be restricted by role and logged for audit purposes. If they need to intervene in an account or override access, that should be allowed for support, security, or policy enforcement, but not casually, and only designated admins should do it. Some actions, like changing roles or deactivating an account, should require approval or at least a second review in special cases, especially if they affect faculty accounts or an active student record. One-off access exceptions are allowed only in exceptional cases, such as troubleshooting a support issue, resolving a grading dispute, or handling an urgent administrative matter, and they require documented approval from an appropriate supervisor or system owner, a clear reason, a time limit, confirmation of exactly which data or function the person can access, and full logging of who approved it, who received it, what they accessed, and when it expired. If unauthorized access or data loss is suspected, the system should immediately contain the issue by disabling the affected account or access path, preserving logs, and preventing any further changes if possible. Support should escalate right away to security and the appropriate NJIT administrators, and any notification to users or leadership should follow the university’s incident response and privacy rules. If there’s data loss, recovery from backup should happen where appropriate, but only after the incident is controlled and the impact is understood. Notification should go to the people who need to respond first, like security, IT support, and the relevant NJIT administrator, and then to affected faculty or students only if the incident actually impacts them. The message should be kept minimal at first, sharing only what’s necessary to explain the issue and any required action, without exposing more student data than needed. If there’s any chance the incident involves privacy or legal implications, communication should be reviewed before it goes out to the broader audience.
